items.title: Announcing Rust 1.100.0
items.summary: The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with:$ rustup update stableIf you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0.If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!What's in 1.100.0 stableNever typeAllocator APIDropGuard APIConjuring zero-sized typesReporting unused dependencies in CargoReducing Cargo cache collisionsCargo min-publish-ageStabilized APIsNever typeAfter 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work.The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !.Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if:fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) {    let value = match option {        // `x` has type `u32`        Some(x) => x,        // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`,        // allowing the `match` to pass type checking.        None => return,    };    // ...}While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (-> !), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T {    // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before    let Ok(v) = res;    v}Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.Allocator APIThis release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait.This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!DropGuard: run a closure on every exit pathThe Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return, ?, or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback.
